newsitem.title: CHINA: HK to become China's first "special" region.
newsitem.headline: HK to become China's first "special" region.

text.p: The British colony of Hong Kong will become China's first Special Administrative Region (SAR) when it returns to Beijing's rule at midnight on Monday.
Following are details of the SAR formula and of the other administrative units China uses to govern its nation of 1.2 billion people:
1. The Hong Kong Special Administrative Region will be unique in China in retaining a separate political and economic system with a high degree of autonomy from Beijing.
-- Institutions such as the central monetary authority, police and local legislature and executive will remain independent of their mainland counterparts.
-- Beijing will control defence and foreign affairs.
2. China has five autonomous regions, operating in areas with significant populations of minority nationality people.

-- These Autonomous Regions, which include the restive Himalayan region of Tibet and the Moslem-dominated northwestern region of Xinjiang, have little more genuine self rule than China's 22 provinces.
-- Regions and provinces all have an executive leader, local Communist Party structure and a People's Congress empowered to pass resolutions on regional affairs.
-- While some decision making is decentralised, provinces and regions have no control over macro-economic policies and all their main institutions are tied to the national leadership.

-- The cities of Beijing, Shanghai, northern Tianjin and southwestern Chongqing are ruled as Municipalities under the Central Government, giving them status equivalent to provinces and direct lines of communication to the national leadership.
3. The Special Administrative Region will also be different from China's existing Special Economic Zones (SEZs), which were set up to boost economic growth in selected areas.

-- SEZs benefit from a range of special tax regimes and favourable economic policies intended to attract foreign investment and to turn them into test-cases and economic powerhouses for the rest of the country.
-- While the zones often enjoy more local economic freedom than ordinary cities or provinces, they are not separated institutionally and are not considered politically autonomous.
